nameStory: Lindley's aster honors John Lindley, a prominent English botanist who first described this species in 1834. Lindley was known for his work on orchids and plant classification, and this northern aster carries his name across the woodlands of Canada and the northern United States. It's also called 'fringed blue aster' for the tiny hairs (cilia) that fringe its leaves - 'ciliolatum' means 'with small hairs' in Latin.
description: Lindley's aster is a perennial wildflower that brings late-season color to northern woodlands with its clusters of small, daisy-like flowers. Each bloom has pale blue to lavender petals (called ray petals) surrounding a bright yellow center, creating the classic aster look. The plant typically grows 1-4 feet tall with heart-shaped leaves and spreads slowly to form small colonies. As a northern species, it's perfectly adapted to cooler climates and woodland conditions.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with fringed edges lined with tiny, soft hairs you can feel when you run your finger along the leaf margin - this gives the plant its scientific name 'ciliolatum' meaning small-haired

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small daisy-like blooms about 1 inch across with 8-20 narrow, pale blue to lavender petals radiating from a bright yellow center, arranged in loose, branching clusters

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 1-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel smooth to slightly rough when touched, often forming small patches through underground rhizomes

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy white seedheads appear after flowering, with small seeds topped by silky white bristles that catch the wind and feel soft like dandelion puffs

habitat: Lindley's aster thrives in moist, rich woodlands and forest edges throughout northern New England, particularly in areas with dappled sunlight. Look for it in deciduous and mixed forests with well-drained but moisture-retentive soils, often growing alongside other woodland wildflowers like wild ginger and trilliums. It prefers cooler, shadier spots than many other asters and is most common in the northern reaches of our region.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes, showing the characteristic heart-shaped leaves with their fringed, hairy margins that help identify the plant even before flowering.
seasonality.summer: Foliage develops fully into lush clumps of heart-shaped leaves, but the plant remains relatively inconspicuous until late summer when flower buds begin forming.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming occurs from August through September, when clusters of pale blue flowers create a soft haze of color, followed by fluffy white seedheads that persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only underground rhizomes to survive the cold - look for dried brown stems and any remaining fluffy seedheads.

funFact: With only one recorded observation in all of New England, Lindley's aster is so rare in our region that finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure - you might be among fewer than a dozen people to ever spot this northern beauty in New England!
confusionNotes: Lindley's aster can be confused with other blue-flowered woodland asters, especially the Common Blue Wood Aster, but the heart-shaped leaves with distinctly fringed, hairy margins are the giveaway. Memory trick: 'Lindley's leaves have hairy edges' - run your finger along the leaf edge to feel the soft fringe that gives this species its scientific name.
contextualKnowledge: This aster represents the northern edge of botanical diversity in New England - it's primarily a Canadian species that just barely reaches into our region. The extremely low observation count suggests it may be at the very southern limit of its range here, making any sighting particularly significant for our understanding of plant distributions.
compareHints: Unlike its common cousin the New England aster with its larger purple flowers and lance-shaped leaves, Lindley's aster has distinctly heart-shaped leaves with fringed edges and smaller, paler blue flowers. It's also much more shade-tolerant than most asters, preferring woodland settings rather than the sunny fields and roadsides where you'd find New England aster or Common Blue Wood Aster. The heart-shaped leaves immediately separate it from nearly all other asters in our region, which typically have narrow or oval leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its many aster relatives, New England aster stands out for its robust size, densely hairy stems, and the distinctive ear-like leaf bases that clasp the stem.
Among its many aster relatives, common blue wood aster stands out with its heart-shaped leaves - most other blue asters like smooth blue aster or New England aster have narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Calico aster stands out from its Symphyotrichum cousins by having much smaller flowers than showy species like New England aster or New York aster.
Among New England's many asters, swamp aster is unique in combining wet habitat preferences with that telltale red-purple stem.
Among New England's many asters, New York aster stands out for its preference for wet habitats and its smooth leaves - many other asters like New England aster have hairy or rough leaves.

Among its many Symphyotrichum relatives, panicled aster stands out for its height and distinctive branching flower arrangement - most other white asters like small white aster have simpler, less elaborate flower clusters.
Among New England's white asters, hairy white oldfield aster stands out for its extremely dense, cloud-like flower clusters and notably fuzzy stems.
Among New England's many asters, perennial saltmarsh aster is unique in its extreme salt tolerance and coastal habitat - no other Symphyotrichum species can survive regular saltwater flooding.
Among its many aster relatives, small white aster stands out for its particularly tiny flowers and smooth stems.
Among New England's many asters, wavy-leaf aster stands out for its distinctive undulating leaf margins - a feature that's much more pronounced than in related species.
Among the white-flowered asters, bushy aster is unique for its extremely compact, mounded growth habit that really does look shrub-like.
Among New England's many asters, white heath aster stands out for its incredibly small, numerous flowers and tiny narrow leaves.
Among its many aster relatives, late purple aster stands out for its extremely open, spreading growth habit - most other Symphyotrichum species grow more upright and dense.
Among New England's many asters, smooth blue aster stands out for its completely hairless, waxy leaves - most other asters have at least some fuzziness.

Among its many aster relatives, annual saltmarsh aster stands out for being truly annual (most others are perennial) and for its extremely small flower heads - much tinier than showy species like New England aster or New York aster.
Eastern silvery aster is easily distinguished from other New England asters by its unique silvery-gray, silky foliage - no other aster in the region has this distinctive texture and color.
Among New England's many Symphyotrichum species, crookedstem aster stands out for its notably thick, often bent stems that turn purple with age.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, Tradescant's aster is distinguished by its coastal preference and salt tolerance, unlike most other Symphyotrichum species that prefer inland habitats.
Among New England's many asters, willowleaf aster stands out for its exceptionally narrow, willow-like leaves - most other Symphyotrichum species have broader, more oval or heart-shaped leaves.
Among its Symphyotrichum relatives in New England, aromatic aster is unique for its distinctive leaf fragrance and relatively uncommon status.
Unlike its robust cousins like New England aster or swamp aster, northern bog aster has a much more delicate, slender build with narrower leaves.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, Ontario aster stands out for its preference for wet bottomlands rather than dry fields or woods.
Among its many aster relatives in New England, shining aster stands out for its exceptionally glossy leaves - most other Symphyotrichum species have fuzzy, rough, or at least matte-finished foliage.
Unlike the robust, hairy New England aster with its deep purple flowers, Anticosti aster is much more delicate with paler blooms.
Unlike its Symphyotrichum relatives such as New England aster or calico aster, rayless annual aster completely lacks ray petals and lives only one year instead of returning each season.
Unlike the heart-shaped leaves of Common Blue Wood Aster or the narrow leaves of panicled aster, arrow-leaved aster's triangular, pointed leaves are unmistakable.
